inflation.shortDef: The steady rise in prices of goods and services over time, which reduces the real purchasing power of your money.
inflation.example: A plate of biryani that cost ₹150 five years ago now costs ₹260. That difference is inflation eroding currency value.

repo-rate.shortDef: The benchmark interest rate at which the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) lends money to commercial banks.
repo-rate.example: When the RBI raises the repo rate, home loans and car EMIs become more expensive, cooling down spending.

cibil-score.shortDef: A 3-digit numerical score between 300 and 900 that grades your creditworthiness and history of repaying debts.
cibil-score.example: A score above 750 gets you fast approval and lower interest rates on loans, whereas a score below 650 indicates high default risk.

nifty-50.shortDef: The flagship stock index representing India's 50 largest, most actively traded blue-chip companies across 13 economic sectors.
nifty-50.example: When news anchors announce 'the Indian market gained 1%', they are usually quoting the day's move in the Nifty 50.

sip.shortDef: An automated investment facility allowing you to invest a fixed amount into mutual funds at regular intervals (usually monthly).
sip.example: Scheduling ₹2,000 to automatically transfer into a Nifty 50 index fund on the 5th of every month is an SIP.

mutual-fund.shortDef: A pooled financial vehicle where money from thousands of investors is managed by professionals to purchase a basket of stocks, bonds, or commodities.
mutual-fund.example: Instead of buying 50 individual corporate shares yourself, you buy units of a mutual fund that owns all of them for you.

index-fund.shortDef: A low-cost mutual fund or ETF that passively replicates a market index like the Nifty 50 without trying to pick individual winning stocks.
index-fund.example: A Nifty 50 Index Fund buys the top 50 Indian companies in the exact same weight as the index, charging minimal management fees.

expense-ratio.shortDef: The annual percentage fee that a mutual fund charges to cover management, administrative, and distribution costs.
expense-ratio.example: An expense ratio of 0.2% on a ₹1,00,000 investment costs ₹200 a year, whereas a 1.5% regular fund charges ₹1,500 every single year.

ctc.shortDef: The total financial expenditure an employer spends on an employee annually, including non-cash benefits and statutory retiral benefits.
ctc.example: A ₹12 Lakh CTC includes employer PF, gratuity accruals, health coverage, and bonus, leaving you with roughly ₹82,000 in monthly take-home.

in-hand-salary.shortDef: The net amount of money that actually gets credited to your bank account on pay day after all taxes and statutory deductions.
in-hand-salary.example: If your gross salary is ₹70,000, your in-hand may be ₹62,000 after ₹4,000 PF contribution, ₹3,800 TDS, and ₹200 professional tax.

emergency-fund.shortDef: A dedicated, easily accessible stash of cash reserved exclusively for unexpected life events like job loss, medical emergencies, or urgent house repairs.
emergency-fund.example: Saving 6 months of mandatory expenses (₹1,80,000 if your survival monthly budget is ₹30,000) stored in a sweep FD or liquid fund.

no-cost-emi.shortDef: A financing scheme where the retailer gives an upfront discount equal to the interest charged by the bank, giving the illusion of zero interest.
no-cost-emi.example: A ₹60,000 phone is discounted to ₹55,000; the bank charges ₹5,000 in interest plus 18% GST on the interest and processing fees.

term-insurance.shortDef: Pure financial protection that pays a guaranteed tax-free lump sum to your family if you pass away during the policy term.
term-insurance.example: A 24-year-old non-smoker can get a ₹1 Crore term life cover for under ₹800 per month.

compounding.shortDef: Earning returns not only on your original invested principal, but also on the accumulated interest and gains from previous periods.
compounding.example: ₹10,000 growing at 10% earns ₹1,000 in year one. In year two, you earn 10% on ₹11,000 (₹1,100), accelerating exponentially over decades.

upi.shortDef: India's real-time payment system developed by NPCI that enables instant money transfers between any two bank accounts via mobile phone.
upi.example: Scanning a QR code at your neighborhood grocery shop to instantly transfer ₹250 directly from your bank account.

nav.shortDef: The per-unit market value of a mutual fund scheme, calculated by dividing the total value of its assets minus liabilities by outstanding units.
nav.example: If a mutual fund owns ₹10 Crore in assets and has 1 Crore units issued, the NAV is ₹10 per unit.

ltcg.shortDef: Profit earned on the sale of an asset or equity security held for longer than the statutory holding threshold (1 year for equity).
ltcg.example: If you buy shares for ₹1 Lakh and sell them for ₹2.5 Lakh after 18 months, your LTCG is ₹1.5 Lakh, taxed at 12.5% on amounts above ₹1.25 Lakh.

stcg.shortDef: Profit realized from selling an asset or equity security before completing the qualifying holding period (under 12 months for equity).
stcg.example: Selling shares at a ₹20,000 profit after holding for 3 months triggers STCG tax at a flat 20% rate.

form-16.shortDef: An official certificate issued by an employer detailing the salary paid, allowances granted, and Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) deposited with the government.
form-16.example: Your HR department issues Form 16 in May or June, which contains the exact figures needed to file your annual Income Tax Return.

itr.shortDef: A prescribed government form submitted annually to the Income Tax Department declaring your income, deductions, and total tax liability.
itr.example: Filing ITR-1 before July 31st each year to report your salary income and claim any excess TDS refunds due.

asset-allocation.shortDef: The strategic division of your investment portfolio across different asset categories such as equity, debt (fixed income), gold, and liquid cash.
asset-allocation.example: A 25-year-old maintaining 70% in Indian equities, 20% in debt instruments, and 10% in gold for risk diversification.

liquid-fund.shortDef: A low-risk debt mutual fund that invests exclusively in ultra-short-term money market instruments with maturity up to 91 days.
liquid-fund.example: Parking your emergency fund in a liquid fund offers better yields than a savings account with instant redemption up to ₹50,000.

dividend.shortDef: A share of profits that a company's board of directors elects to distribute directly to its shareholders in cash.
dividend.example: If a company declares a dividend of ₹10 per share and you own 100 shares, you receive ₹1,000 directly into your bank account.

dicgc.shortDef: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, an RBI subsidiary that insures bank deposits up to ₹5,00,000 per depositor per bank.
dicgc.example: If your bank becomes insolvent, DICGC guarantees reimbursement of your deposits up to ₹5 Lakh within 90 days.

ais.shortDef: A comprehensive statement generated by the tax department tracking all your financial transactions, interest earnings, dividends, and share sales.
ais.example: Checking your AIS before filing taxes ensures you don't forget to report interest from hidden savings accounts.

ppf.shortDef: A government-backed 15-year long-term savings scheme offering guaranteed, tax-free interest under the EEE (Exempt-Exempt-Exempt) tax category.
ppf.example: Depositing ₹1.5 Lakh annually into PPF locks money in for 15 years with zero tax on contribution, zero tax on interest, and zero tax on withdrawal.
